The bill would strengthen Australia's counter-terrorism laws to address threats from Australians who fight or train with extremist groups overseas.
It would give security agencies extra powers, improve border security, and cancel welfare payments for people involved in terrorism.

The bill implements recommendations from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor's second and fourth annual reports and the Council of Australian Governments Review of Counter-Terrorism Legislation.
Give security agencies additional powers to deal with terrorism within Australia and by Australians overseas.

The majority did not want to change the exceptions to the offence of entering and staying in a declared area. Labor Senator [Penny Wong](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/penny_wong) had proposed to delete the current exceptions and replace them with an [exception](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2014-10-29.57.1) of "entering or remaining for a legitimate purpose". ###Enter or stay in declared area offence The bill will make it an offence for someone to enter or stay in an area that the [Minister for Foreign Affairs](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/curtin/julie_bishop) declares as a declared area. A whole country can be a declared area, which was [criticised](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-10-17/parliamentary-committee-recommends-passing-of-foreign-fighters-/5821514) by the [Joint Parliamentary Committee on Intelligence and Security](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Joint_Committee_on_Intelligence_and_Security). The current exceptions to this offence (in [proposed subsection 119.2(3)](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;db=LEGISLATION;id=legislation%2Fbills%2Fs976_first-senate%2F0001;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbills%2Fs976_first-senate%2F0001%22;rec=0)) include when a person is involved in: * [humanitarian aid](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarian_aid) (but this has to be the sole act), * a court case, * work for an Australian government (state or federal), * work for a foreign government (so long as it's not violating Australian law), * work for the [United Nations](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations), * journalism, and * visiting a family member. Read more about this new offence in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd034). ###Background to the bill A number of incidents happened before and after this bill's introduction. Presented the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights' examination of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Foreign Fighters) Bill 2014, concluding that its declared area offence, carrying up to 10 years imprisonment, is likely incompatible with human rights because it reverses the presumption of innocence, and raised concerns about a new advocating terrorism offence that could criminalise speech through a recklessness test.

Moved the second reading of the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Foreign Fighters) Bill 2014, which would expand counter-terrorism powers and offences, strengthen border and travel controls, and enable agencies to address returning foreign fighters while providing review and other safeguards.

Supported constructive bipartisan action on the foreign fighters bill while arguing that Labor should not provide a blank cheque, describing committee scrutiny and negotiated safeguards concerning new offences, declared areas, biometric information and the duration of coercive powers.

Argued that the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (Foreign Fighters) Bill 2014 would remove rights, criminalise innocent travel to declared areas and expand detention and biometric powers, and proposed amendments protecting journalists, requiring harmful intent and preserving proper scrutiny.
